articles.title_orig: California woman indicted on charges that she was spying for China
articles.title_zh: California woman indicted on charges that she was spying for China
articles.content_orig:
A California woman who prosecutors allege was spying on a son of Taiwan’s president was indicted this month on charges of conspiracy and being an unregistered foreign agent for China.
The indictment was filed Oct. 9 in U.S. District Court for the Central District of California, and the allegations it lays out mirror an earlier criminal complaint against the woman, Wanying Zhang, 34, of Irvine.
Prosecutors say Zhang, who also goes by Heather, spied on a son of Taiwan’s president outside his home in the Seattle area at the behest of Chinese officials. The spying is alleged to have taken place between roughly June and September 2025, prosecutors claim.
Taiwan is a self-ruled democracy that is the source of 90% of the world’s “leading-edge chip manufacturing,” according to the U.S. International Trade Administration . China claims Taiwan, which the U.S. has recognized for nearly half a century, though it is required by law to ensure Taiwan can defend itself.
Prosecutors allege Zhang was under the direction of an unnamed Chinese government official and former classmate at her alma mater, China’s University of International Relations, which is “closely affiliated with China’s intelligence apparatus,” an FBI investigator said in earlier court documents.
An example of the alleged activity was a request by the former classmate to send him pictures “of the house” where the son lives, according to the indictment.
Prosecutors alleged that Zhang flew from California to Las Vegas and then to the Seattle area to conduct surveillance of the unidentified son and his home from outside.
The indictment alleges she captured photos, video and license plate information and sent them to the person alleged to be her Chinese handler. An unidentified person, who had fled to China in September, was with her, prosecutors said.
Zhang also traveled to China in August 2025 to meet with a Chinese government official, returned days later and told the official she would most likely be going to where the victim was the following week, according to the indictment.
Her lawyer, Craig Harbaugh, did not immediately respond to a request for comment Sunday.
Previously, Harbaugh, a veteran criminal defense attorney, described Zhang as an upstanding resident of Irvine, about 42 miles southeast of Los Angeles, where she lives with her husband and two young daughters.
“The government’s theory — she’s been a sleeper agent for the last 10 years, working as a real estate agent, raising her family and will choose to go to China and abandon her work, her family and her home — it’s not supported,” Harbaugh said in court Oct. 7.
U.S. Magistrate Judge Steve Kim ordered Zhang held in pretrial detention after prosecutors argued she poses a flight risk. The U.S. Bureau of Prisons website shows that she remains in custody.
Zhang is scheduled to appear in federal district court Friday for a post-indictment arraignment. She could face up to 15 years in prison.
David Douglas is a supervising producer for NBC News based in Los Angeles.
Dennis Romero is a breaking news reporter for NBC News Digital.

articles.title_orig: Nasdaq futures gain as investors buy the dip in the AI trade: Live updates
articles.title_zh: Nasdaq futures gain as investors buy the dip in the AI trade: Live updates
articles.content_orig:
Stock futures rebounded on Sunday night as traders cautiously dipped a toe back in following last week's rout in shares linked to the artificial intelligence trend.
Nasdaq-100 futures added 0.4%. Dow Jones Industrial Average futures ticked 0.2% higher, or 110 points. S&P 500 futures gained 0.2%.
Stable oil prices early Sunday also lent the equity market some support.
In Asia, Japan's Nikkei 225 lost 1.65%, while the Topix was down 1.12% on Monday. South Korea's Kospi was 1.29% lower, while the small-cap Kosdaq Index fell 0.93%. Australia's S&P/ASX 200 was up 0.37%.
The S&P 500 lost nearly 2% last week, its biggest weekly decline since late June. The Nasdaq tumbled 4.5%, snapping a four-week winning streak.
Concerns around the health of the AI trade took center stage after CNBC reported, citing sources, that Anthropic's third-quarter revenue totaled $16.8 billion . And while that's up from $11.6 billion in the second quarter, it raised flags among investors about the pace of growth with the AI build-out.
Neocloud stock CoreWeave, which uses large amounts of debt to build data centers that it rents out to tech companies, was at the center of those fears. The AI-linked name plummeted 25% last week — its largest one-week drop since November 2025. Investors in the corporate bond market have started to shun CoreWeave, with the company's credit default swaps reaching distress levels .
It's not just CoreWeave whose moves in the credit market are concerning. Goldman Sachs traders noted Friday: "AI Credit Spreads and hyperscalers specifically are at the widest levels of the year. The last time spreads were nearly this high, the underlying equities were 15% lower."
"The widening across the complex has forced investors to confront what happens as AI spending growth slows. AI Capex has likely peaked and financing, sustainability, and returns on capital have become the debate rather than the next near term earnings revision," they said. "Pessimism is increasing, market breadth is low, and [Friday] we saw the second highest amount of puts traded (right behind June of this year)."
Traders were also keeping a wary eye on oil with ship attacks in the Persian Gulf picking up and Ukraine and Russia trading attacks on energy infrastructure. Ukraine hit an oil terminal in St. Petersburg, Russia on Sunday. Longer-dated oil futures have begun to ratchet higher on expectations energy infrastructure disruptions may last well into 2027.
On Sunday however, Brent and WTI crude futures were both trading a tad lower.
A slew of earnings from major companies such as Meta Platforms and Tesla hit the Street this week with optimism those results will stabilize the market.
Asia-Pacific markets fell Monday, with Japanese stocks leading declines in the region.
Japan's Nikkei 225 lost 1.65%,  while the Topix was down 1.12%.
South Korea's Kospi was 1.29% lower, while the small-cap Kosdaq Index fell 0.93%.
Australia's S&P/ASX 200 was up 0.37%.
Shares of Australia's Cleanaway Waste Management surged 19.84% on Monday after Swedish private equity firm EQT announced an agreement to acquire the company in a deal valued at about $9.3 billion Australian dollars ($6.5 billion).
Under the agreement, EQT will acquire all outstanding shares of Cleanaway for A$3.095 per share in cash, subject to adjustments for any dividends or other distributions.
The offer represents a 32.1% premium to Cleanaway's closing share price of A$2.37 on Aug. 12, the last full trading day before the company first disclosed a potential transaction.
EQT said it sees opportunities to invest in Cleanaway's infrastructure and improve the performance of its waste management network to meet Australia's evolving waste management needs.
Cleanaway's board unanimously recommended that shareholders vote in favor of the deal, citing the significant premium and certainty of cash consideration, subject to no superior proposal emerging and an independent expert concluding that the transaction is in shareholders' best interests.
Asia-Pacific markets were set for a subdued Monday as investors weighed renewed threats from Iran .
Japan's Nikkei 225 was also set to fall at open, with its Chicago and Osaka futures contracts last at 63,985 and 63,630 respectively, compared with the index's previous close of 65,324.29.
Australia's S&P/ASX 200 was up 0.29% in early trade. Hong Kong market is closed for a holiday.
A senior Iranian security official said Sunday that Tehran had drawn up a new military response strategy in the event of further U.S.-Israeli strikes, amid reports of multiple attacks on commercial ships in waters surrounding the Arabian Peninsula.
“Iran’s armed forces have prepared a response to any new act of adventurism that would be far more devastating than the 12-day and 40-day wars,” Mohsen Rezaei, secretary of Iran’s Supreme National Security Council, said in a post on X.
Correction: This post has been revised to reflect that Hong Kong market is closed for a holiday.
Oil prices fell slightly in early trading Sunday even after Ukraine attacked crude facilities in Russia, while more tankers along the Persian Gulf came under attack as well.
Brent crude slipped 1% to $108.80 per barrel. U.S. oil prices lost 0.2% to $101.18.
Fires broke out at an oil terminal and depot in St. Petersburg after Ukraine launched a massive wave of drone strikes on Sunday, St. Petersburg Gov. Alexander Beglov said in a post. Meanwhile, two tankers were attacked off the coast of Saudi Arabia in the Persian Gulf on Friday, according to incident reports from the United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations Centre.
For more on the oil market, read our story here.
Nasdaq-100 futures added 0.4%. Dow Jones Industrial Average futures ticked 0.2% higher, or 110 points. S&P 500 futures gained 0.2%.

articles.title_orig: EU tariffs aimed at China hitting Ukraine, steel boss says
articles.title_zh: EU tariffs aimed at China hitting Ukraine, steel boss says
articles.content_orig:
The boss of one of Ukraine's biggest steel companies has called on the European Union to drop import restrictions on products made from the country, arguing it has been "bundled together" in measures aimed a curbing cheap imports from the likes of China.
Yuriy Ryzhenkov, chief executive of Metinvest, told the BBC the recently-imposed tariffs on imported steel to the EU were "unfair" and had been put in place "without any consideration for the situation Ukraine is in".
He said he wished to see "at least a carve out" for Ukraine to access the EU market.
A spokesperson for the European Commission said the EU "took into account the difficult situation" of Ukraine when deciding its steel policy.
The trading bloc has recently imposed restrictions on steel imports in an effort to protect steel manufacturers of member nations.
It has capped the amount of steel which can enter the EU tax free at 18.3 million tonnes per year - a 47% reduction from 2024 levels.
There are some country-specific quotas in the policy, but the overall aim is to cut the amount of steel that can be imported due to member nations struggling to compete with cheap imports from the likes of China and Turkey.
Despite a free-trade agreement (FTA) being in place between the EU and Ukraine, the FTA does not stop the EU from introducing separate trade protection measures.
"Ukraine has been bundled together into those measures without any consideration for the situation Ukraine is in," Ryzhenkov said, pointing to the war with Russia.
"Access to the European market is crucial for survival," he added. "The restrictive measures that have been put in place by the authorities in the European Union, they don't help.
"I think it's unfair that Ukraine has been treated in the same way as all of the other importers into the European Union."
The Ukraine steel industry estimates steel exports to the EU could ultimately fall by about 50–60%.
The EU said Ukraine's specific steel quota guaranteed exports of the metal, but acknowledged this was at a "level lower than in the past years".
"Despite the war effort, Ukraine remains an important exporter of steel to the EU," a spokesperson said, adding it had "offered compensations" to its largest suppliers, which included Ukraine.
Steel products are a foundation in Ukraine's economy. Before the start of Russia's full-scale invasion in 2022, metallurgy and mining accounted for roughly 10% of Ukraine's national income and a third of its exports. The EU is its top customer.
But the industry has suffered from the continued Russian bombardment.
All of Ukraine's steel mills have been bombed at points since the conflict began in 2022, but Ryzhenkov said strikes had "intensified significantly recently".
At one point in September, there was "no single tonne of steel produced" in Ukraine for the first time in about 150 years, he added.
Almost 800 Metinvest workers have been killed since the war began.
Ryzhenkov said the company had "improved the covered areas" at its mills where workers can shelter during air raids.
"The only thing we can do is to design procedures to keep people safe and just obey those procedures and try to minimise the risks."
"Unfortunately, you cannot cover a whole steel mill to avoid it being damaged."
Ryzhenkov said he expected the coming winter to be "one of the hardest in our history".
"We are in a dire situation when we don't have logistics to access any other market apart from the EU and cutting our available market by 60%, that doesn't help for the industry to survive."

articles.title_orig: An Xbox Series X Can Now Run PlayStation 5 Games, But There's A Catch
articles.title_zh: An Xbox Series X Can Now Run PlayStation 5 Games, But There's A Catch
articles.content_orig:
What is the PS5X Emulator for Xbox Series X and how does it work?
In a YouTube video that went live on September 8, developer Devran Cosmo Uenal booted the PlayStation 5 version of Quake II on an Xbox Series X and played it with an Xbox controller. But the game was running through PS5X, Uenal's Xbox port of the open-source PS5 emulator KytyPS5, and he has gotten three more PS5 games working alongside it.
The fact that he's managed to get PS5 games running on an Xbox at all is super cool, but there's a catch: PS5X only works in the console's official Developer Mode, where Microsoft's documentation caps games at 5GB of memory. That unfortunately rules out the majority of current-gen games, and there's no public download for anyone else to try yet.
Sony and Microsoft built their current consoles around closely matched AMD hardware. Both of them have eight Zen 2 CPU cores, RDNA 2 graphics and 16GB of GDDR6 memory, and PS5 games are compiled for the same x86-64 processor architecture that PCs use. That means the KytyPS5 emulator can run their code on the host CPU instead of recreating the PS5's hardware in software. Its developer calls it a compatibility layer and, practically, it behaves more like a translator, converting what a PS5 game asks for into something a PC can understand.
KytyPS5 translates the PS5's graphics commands and recompiles its shaders for Vulkan. As a result, it needs a Vulkan 1.3 graphics card on PC, but Xbox Developer Mode only supports DirectX 11 and DirectX 12. "Since Vulkan isn't supported, everything needs to be translated to DirectX," Uenal wrote in the YouTube video's description, where he also admitted that AI was involved in the work. As VideoCardz pointed out, that means fixes the KytyPS5 team makes to its PC renderer have to be adapted before PS5X can use them.
Uenal's video also describes PS5X as a "research project" for "running PS5 homebrew and game backups" on a Series X in Developer Mode. He claims that it doesn't include any PS5 firmware or decryption keys, and KytyPS5's documentation tells users to stick to game files they've obtained legally. Dodging copy protection is ultimately what killed the Switch emulator Yuzu, whose makers settled a Nintendo lawsuit back in 2024 by paying $2.4 million and shutting the project down. The team behind the PS3 emulator RPCS3 lists KytyPS5 and SharpEmu as the two active open-source PS5 emulators that can boot games, and warns players about scam sites posing as real ones.
At the time of writing, PS5X runs the PS5 versions of GEX Trilogy , Hellboy: Web of Wyrd , Marvel Cosmic Invasion and Quake II , and all four are compatible with Xbox controller inputs. Some of them have working sound, and TweakTown reckons that Quake II runs at roughly 25 to 45 frames per second in Uenal's footage. It's worth noting that these four games are also sold on other platforms, so there's no sign yet of PS5X running a PS5 exclusive, and Uenal admits that it's early days and that compatibility is limited.
Android Authority reported on September 28 that KytyPS5 now goes in-game in a variety of PS5 titles on PC, and that one user had shown Marvel's Wolverine reaching its main menu, in slow motion, on a machine with an NVIDIA RTX 5090. That clip didn't show any gameplay, however, and it's not clear whether it used the standard emulator build. PS5 emulation on PC is becoming more viable by the week, but it's still an extremely nascent field, and PS5X only inherits any progress once each fix has been rebuilt for DirectX and squeezed into a far smaller memory budget.
Microsoft limits games in Developer Mode to a relatively small 5GB of memory, and apps to 1GB. Requests for more memory than that allocation fail. In contrast, a retail Series X game gets 13.5GB of the console's 16GB, while the remainder is reserved for the console's OS. That leaves PS5X to work with about 37 percent of the memory a normal Xbox game can use, making it an obvious no-go for big current-gen releases. Microsoft only lifts this cap when software runs via the Visual Studio debugger, which is a setup designed for devs testing their code.
Microsoft blocked emulators entirely in Xbox's normal retail mode back in 2023, its rationale for doing so being a store policy that bans products that emulate a game system. It then started bringing down the ban hammer and reportedly handed out 15-day suspensions to players who found a workaround. Since then, players who want to play PS2 or GameCube games through, say, Dolphin, the most popular GameCube emulator , have had to rely on Developer Mode instead. But a console in that mode can't load retail games until it's switched back.
Xbox Series X comes with the same Zen 2 architecture and RDNA 2 graphics as a PS5. It's also got the same amount of memory, and PS5X can use less than a third of that. But none of this really matters because of the memory cap. There's no real workaround to this without a jailbreak, meaning Xbox players won't benefit from the progress being made on the PC. Sure, PS5X is interesting, but it'll remain a cool little curio rather than anything substantive players can use.
If you're interested in checking out PS5X and similar emulation projects, you should exercise caution. Scammers are capitalizing on the interest these projects receive, such as releasing malware under similar names like PCS5X to try and trick players into downloading it.

articles.title_orig: Anthropic commits 5% of shares to new public benefit fund that could address AI job disruption
articles.title_zh: Anthropic commits 5% of shares to new public benefit fund that could address AI job disruption
articles.content_orig:
Anthropic said Sunday it plans to commit 5% of its shares to a new public benefit fund , with the stake potentially increasing as the company's valuation grows.
Subject to shareholder approval, the fund would immediately commit 5% of Anthropic's shares, with the board adding, at its discretion, an additional 2% for every 50% increase in the company's value above a set baseline that has yet to be disclosed.
Anthropic said that while it has already committed $200 million to study the AI's effects, "given the pace of AI progress, bolder approaches may be needed."
The fund may be used to "explore large donations" — including to traditional nonprofits or as direct distributions for specific populations — or for "bolder approaches" to study and address AI's disruption and displacement of jobs, the company said.
An August Pew Research Center report found that 71% of adults think AI will lead to fewer jobs in the U.S. over the next two years.
The fund will be established as a wholly owned limited liability company rather than a 501(c)(3) tax-exempt nonprofit or other format to adjust between different forms of giving, the release said. Equity held by the LLC will not be used for lobbying or political giving in the U.S. or internationally, Anthropic said.
Anthropic told investors its third-quarter revenue stands at $16.8 billion ahead of its planned initial public offering reportedly slated for November, CNBC reported .
The timing of Anthropic's public fund announcement is both mandatory to prepare for an initial public offering, and "beneficial from an image perspective," especially as AI reshapes the jobs market, Lise Buyer, partner at IPO advisory firm Class V Group, told CNBC.
Buyer said Anthropic's move could be seen favorably if the funds support retraining or help workers find alternative employment when the technology disrupts their jobs.
"Of course, it is also to burnish their reputation at a time when AI is coming under significant scrutiny," she added.
Anthropic said it will share more about the fund structure and governance in the coming months, including valuation milestones that may increase the stake. It said it will also share progress on the fund in an upcoming public benefit report.
In response to Anthropic's announcement, Tesla and SpaceX CEO Elon Musk said on X that he "recommend[s] giving the shares directly to the public."

articles.title_orig: France in Shock After Protests Turn Into Riots, Damaging Buildings and Shops
articles.title_zh: France in Shock After Protests Turn Into Riots, Damaging Buildings and Shops
articles.content_orig:
France’s President Emmanuel Macron addressed the nation on Sunday evening as communities reeled from one of the most violent nights of unrest in recent years after largely peaceful anti-government protests descended into rioting, leaving government buildings torched, one police officer and one protester dead.
Macron said that the full force of the law would be brought to bear on those who had damaged property or participated in rioting.
“Those who destroyed must pay,” Macron said. “Those who looted must pay back. Those who sought to bring down the Republic will be held accountable.”
Macron described the violence as the work of “seditious elements from far-left factions, joined by numerous delinquents.”
“Watching these images, we were all wondering: what had got into them? How can French people do that to France?”
“Nothing can justify it, explain it or excuse it,” Macron said. “Tonight we all feel both anger and shame.”
The president added that the government should listen to public grievances, and that many protesters did not participate in violence.
“Yesterday, hundreds of thousands of our compatriots demonstrated to state legitimate claims,” Macron said. “Never must we confuse the latter with those who destroyed and vandalized.”
Macron said that he had asked the government to convene stakeholders – including students, teachers, trade unionists and others – this week to discuss “concrete proposals.”
There were at least two deaths connected to rioting and protests over the weekend. A 22-year-old police officer died after being “struck by a third-party vehicle” in the city of Nantes, about 250 miles southwest of Paris, France’s Interior Minister Laurent Nunez said .
One protester died just north of Paris following a “cardiorespiratory arrest,” CNN affiliate BFMTV reported on Sunday , citing the Paris Police headquarters.
Police have detained more than 2,000 people, Nunez said, adding that more than 600 police officers were injured.
Scenes unfolded again on Sunday of police officers launching tear gas into the hallowed Place de la République, where dozens of people gathered in response to messages on social media to “continue the movement,” BFMTV reported. In the central city of Limoges, the 143-year-old town hall was set ablaze on Saturday, with video showing its spire collapsing. In Marseille, masked protesters dressed all in black broke into city hall and defaced the building, and in Lyon, protesters torched the city’s tourist office.
Lawmakers and regional officials launched mounting criticism over the government’s law enforcement plan, BFMTV said, with French Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu set to meet the mayors of Paris, Lyon and Marseille, who called for greater reinforcement to repair the damage.
As night fell in Paris on Saturday, groups of young people looted shops and started fires as protests wound down, prompting police to respond with tear gas and baton charges in the narrow streets. Alexandre Bompard, CEO of retail giant Carrefour, said in a social media post Sunday that around 1,500 stores across the country were affected by violence.
More than 600 police officers have been injured, France’s Interior Minister Laurent Nunez posted on X on Sunday, warning that “nothing can justify” the unrest. Earlier this weekend, Lecornu also condemned “unacceptable levels of violence.”
The destruction followed what had been largely peaceful protests, which have grown out of sweeping student-led rallies that gripped parts of France last month, sparking a broader movement against crumbling schools, the spiking cost of living, and perceived government inaction. The rallies have become emblematic of long-simmering, intergenerational anger among people who say their calls for social and political change are going unmet by negligent governments.
Some 550,000 protesters hit the streets across France, including 110,000 in Paris, Nunez said on Saturday. Organizers said far more people turned out.
“There’s an accumulation of wealth and power that’s completely out of control,” one protester, who gave her name as Pauline, told CNN in Paris on Saturday.
“We’re also here to support the youth. There are victories, but if we look at the bigger picture, it’s not going in the right direction,” the 36-year-old added.
Another demonstrator complained of “less democracy” and a “concentration of power” under Macron’s leadership. “There are billionaires who control the media,” Louise, 38, told CNN. “We are fighting to change things.”
Macron slammed “sowers of chaos” for interfering with peaceful protests, and warned late on Saturday that “those who have broken, attacked (police) prefectures, as well as businesses, looted even our town halls, will be prosecuted and punished.”
“We do not back down in the face of rioters and those who’ve come to attack law enforcement,” said the Paris Police Prefecture – the body that oversees the Paris Police Force, emergency services and various other administrative departments – adding that its staffers stood “their ground with courage and professionalism.”
The police response to the weeks of protest has come under scrutiny. Earlier in the week, that response had left a 14-year-old boy with a fractured jaw. Another police officer was captured on camera using a headlock on a girl in the northwestern area of Alençon, an action now prohibited by law.
A protester in the city of Saint-Étienne, about 40 miles southwest of Lyon, lost his hand during a march there on Saturday, a police source told BFMTV.
This is the second reported instance of a demonstrator losing their hand in the current wave of student protests.
A student in the northeastern city of Lens lost his hand after reportedly picking up a grenade earlier this month, prompting the temporary suspension of one type of stun grenade by police. That ban, which still allowed police to use several different grenades, has now been rescinded.
Overall, authorities said that the “vast majority of individuals” had demonstrated peacefully on Saturday, according to BFMTV.
Posting on X, Jean-Luc Mélenchon, leader of the far-left La France Insoumise Party, emphasized that the majority of demonstrators on Sunday had made their point peacefully. “While news channels are flooded with images of violence in dozens of cities, everything is unfolding peacefully with tens of thousands of people calmly mobilized. Two worlds, two realities.”
Youth activists also led solidarity protests in Belgium, Albania and Italy , where police arrested more than 70 people for identification in the city of Milan on Sunday, according to CNN affiliate SkyTG24.
Reuters reported Sunday that police in Milan clashed with stone-throwing demonstrators for a second day, with law enforcement firing tear gas and water cannons in response. SkyTG24 shared video from a supermarket in Milan, showing the windows smashed out and merchandise scattered over the floor after looting.
Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni condemned the looting in a statement posted on social media, and said that she will convene a meeting in Rome on Monday to “evaluate further measures against those who exploit legitimate demonstrations to sow violence and chaos.”
The wave of protests in France has its roots in the country’s public school system. Earlier this fall, French high school students organized scattered protests demanding reduced class sizes, increased spending on teachers, investments in infrastructure designed to withstand the climate crisis and an end to police violence against young people.
In the past decade and a half, a rise in fertility coupled with funding cuts has led to more students, but fewer teachers in classrooms. The French Education Minister Edouard Geffray has met with student protesters multiple times in recent weeks, although an agreement is yet to be made.
This story has been updated with additional information.

articles.title_orig: Priest in Ecuador dies after crucifix falls on him during livestreamed Mass
articles.title_zh: Priest in Ecuador dies after crucifix falls on him during livestreamed Mass
articles.content_orig:
A priest in Ecuador died Saturday after a crucifix fell on him during a livestreamed Mass, according to church officials and video of the incident.
The Rev. Patricio Alfredo Sánchez Molinari died Saturday, the Archdiocese of Guayaquil announced.
He was the parish priest at the Church of Perpetual Relief of the Central Vicariate, the archdiocese said.
Molinari “has left to the House of the Father to enjoy his presence and glory,” it said in a news release.
The Mass was livestreamed, but the video was taken down. The video, reviewed by NBC News, showed a large crucifix hanging on a wall behind Molinari suddenly falling forward onto the back of his head.
Molinari was behind the altar, facing the congregation, and did not see the crucifix falling behind him.
Molinari did not stand back up, and parishioners are heard on the video shrieking and crying. Some rush to tend to him.
A Eucharist in his memory is scheduled for Sunday evening.
Marlene Lenthang is a breaking news reporter for NBC News Digital.
Maya Rosenberg is an assignment editor based in Miami.

articles.title_orig: 4 dead, dozens wounded after large fire breaks out at Canadian military base, officials say
articles.title_zh: 4 dead, dozens wounded after large fire breaks out at Canadian military base, officials say
articles.content_orig:
Four service members were killed in an incident at a military base in the Canadian province of Alberta, which caused a major fire, Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney said Sunday. Dozens of others were seriously wounded, he added.
Carney said he'd requested a detailed account and formal briefing on the incident at Canadian Forces Base (CFB) Wainwright, which senior officials on the ground at the site were expected to deliver later on Sunday.
Alberta Premier Danielle Smith said Sunday that 39 patients were still hospitalized and at least 19 were in critical condition.
Smith said patients were transferred from Canadian Forces Base Wainwright to four hospitals across Alberta. She said some suffered severe burns and could face weeks or months of intensive treatment.
After the incident happened on Saturday, a doctor at a hospital in the city of Edmonton, 120 miles northwest of the military base, told Canada's national broadcaster that patients were being brought to hospitals across the city as health care facilities around the base became "completely overwhelmed" by the number of people needing care.
"This number of patients would overwhelm the city of Edmonton," Dr. Warren Thirsk, an emergency department physician at the Royal Alexandra Hospital, told CBC News. "It is more patients than any of us want to count right now. It's a disaster. It's a one in every 15 to 25-year disaster."
"I'm saddened to share that there have been both fatalities and injuries as a result of an incident on the base," Defense Minister David McGuinty said.
The incident occurred at Canadian Forces Base Wainwright, located about 112 miles southeast of Edmonton.
Major-General Wade Rutland, commander of 1st Canadian Division, said Sunday a grass fire broke out during a training exercise and spread quickly. He said the cause of the initial fire is still under investigation, noting there were "multiple training activities happening throughout the training area at the time."
Rutland said the fire crossed "established fire guards" before it was contained with the help of local authorities. He also said reports of explosions were not believed to be the result of the fire reaching oil and gas infrastructure or from "any outside interference."
Firefighters faced a volatile situation. Large areas of the province were hit during the day by a windstorm with gusts up to 100 kilometers (62 miles) an hour. The wind toppled some trees and sent signs flying and garbage cans rolling down streets.
By 11 p.m., the Municipal District of Wainwright said on social media the fire was being held and that property and critical infrastructure were protected. There was no evacuation order for residents.
McGuinty said the Royal Canadian Mounted Police were involved in the investigation and described the situation as "very, very active and delicate."
"I cannot recall such an incident in my short time for sure as a minister, but I cannot recall an incident like this in recent memory," McGuinty said.
The Canadian Armed Forces and federal, provincial and local authorities were coordinating the emergency response, he said. The nearby community of Wainwright was providing hospital and firefighting support.
"Our thoughts are with all the brave women and men affected," Carney said earlier in a social media post.
Smith described the fire as "significant and tragic" and said it was affecting many military personnel.
Canadian Forces Base Wainwright is one of Canada's busiest military training bases, where soldiers prepare for combat operations. It is home to the Canadian Manoeuvre Training Centre, which conducts realistic battlefield exercises, and the 3rd Canadian Division Training Centre, which provides military training.
Carney said the federal government was working closely with Alberta officials and local authorities. He said he and Smith were in close contact, as were their ministers and officials.
Smith thanked first responders and those providing care and support to those affected.
Canadian Conservative opposition leader Pierre Poilievre said he had spoken with Carney and the defense minister to offer support to those affected by the fire.
"Pray for Wainwright, everyone," Poilievre said in a social media post. He urged people in the area to follow emergency instructions and keep roads clear for first responders.
The fire came days before the province is set to vote on beginning a process that could lead to its seeking independence from Canada.

articles.title_orig: AI Cloud Firm Nscale Faces Investor Pushback Over IPO Valuation
articles.title_zh: AI Cloud Firm Nscale Faces Investor Pushback Over IPO Valuation
articles.content_orig:
A tech company has said it still plans to build the UK's largest AI data centre despite Microsoft pulling out of the project.
Nscale announced last year it had pledged £2bn to build and open a pioneering facility in Loughton , Essex.
However, the BBC understands that Microsoft, which said it would fund a supercomputer at the site, has terminated its involvement.
A spokesperson for Nscale said it was exploring alternative power sources and its relationship with Microsoft remained strong for their other projects together overseas. Microsoft declined to comment.
"We remain committed to both the Loughton project and the UK and we are exploring alternative power sources for the site, in addition to other expansion sites in the UK," Nscale said.
"Our relationship with Microsoft remains strong and long-term."
The data centre was due to receive its power supply at the end of the year.
But as first reported by the Telegraph on Sunday , Nscale has been told this will not happen until the 2030s.
"This unfortunate London-wide grid issue has no impact on our other contracts," Nscale told the BBC.
Nscale and Microsoft are still working together on projects in Norway, Portugal and the United States.
The Loughton site is expected to create 250 permanent jobs when it eventually opens.
Only last month, Microsoft announced that some of the $30bn (£22bn) it was investing in the UK would be used to fund the Loughton supercomputer.

articles.title_orig: Jet skids off runway after botched takeoff at Las Vegas airport
articles.title_zh: Jet skids off runway after botched takeoff at Las Vegas airport
articles.content_orig:
A private jet aborted its takeoff after it ran off the end of a runway at Harry Reid International Airport Sunday morning.
The aircraft, a Dassault Falcon 50 with tail number N200SG, was departing from Runway 1L at about 11 a.m. when it skidded off the runway and made contact with the airport’s perimeter fence.
“At approximately 11 a.m., upon departure, a general aviation aircraft skid off runway 1L at LAS and made contact with the perimeter fence. There are no known injuries at this time,” the airport said.
“Runways 1R and 1L will be closed for inspection, and travelers may experience some delays. We will provide updates as more information becomes available,” authorities said.
A flight-tracking map shared on social media by Red Wave Press shows the jet moving slowly from its taxi position and turning onto the runway.
The plane then continues past the end of the pavement before veering to the right and coming to a complete stop. The airport said the aircraft made contact with the perimeter fence.
The Federal Aviation Administration has issued a ground stop for the airport, citing an “aircraft emergency.” Airport officials said the stop may result in delays and urged travelers to check with their airlines about flight status.
FAA registry records show that the aircraft, a three-engine business jet, is owned by Jacks Wings LLC of Boca Raton, Florida.

articles.title_orig: Emmanuel Macron faces political firestorm after riots
articles.title_zh: Emmanuel Macron faces political firestorm after riots
articles.content_orig:
Henry's 2023 Sarkozy-Gaddafi trial coverage was cited in the European Parliament’s anti-corruption resolution, and the French culture ministry referenced his Louvre funding analysis during its 2025 budget negotiations
On Sunday morning, the City of Love resembled a City of Hate.
Trucks and cars lay smouldering, bus shelters were smashed, and mounds of melted bins and Lime bikes littered the typically picturesque avenues and boulevards.
Most shocking were the dozens of shops where metal shutters had been prised open, window panes smashed, and stores looted to the last item.
Similar scenes of chaos had played out in Marseille, Lyon and other big cities. In Limoges, the 19th-century bell tower came crashing down in flames in an eerie reminder of the Notre-Dame blaze. This time, however, the damage was deliberate.
“It’s a war zone,” lamented Mehmet, a retired tailor of Turkish origin who has lived in Paris “since de Gaulle was still alive”. “We’re the ones who’ll end up paying for all this. It’s unacceptable. France isn’t what it used to be.”
It all started festively enough.
Parents and teachers marched with pupils and students manning carnival-like floats – a huge Trojan horse passed by my front door – as Yellow Vests and unions joined the fray to protest against rising living costs and for “social justice” .
It is arguably uplifting to seeing your children peacefully demonstrate for a better world and vent their anger at a tide of existential threats from war to climate change and AI.
It is tragic to see their genuine concerns eclipsed by mindless anarchy.
As the government has said, it was a “miracle” no one died. In fact, two did, one from a seizure during the Paris protest, a second falling from atop the Arc de Triomphe.
The police, who have been the main butt of young protesters’ fury for their alleged brutality, were completely overwhelmed and at times absent.
Benoit Payan, Marseille’s mayor, asked why he had just one company of national riot police for a city 2.5 times the area of Paris. It felt almost as if officers had vanished to teach France a lesson.
The Left and Greens called for Laurent Nunez, the interior minister, to resign.
Some foreign leaders gleefully weaponised the chaos.
“ France is burning ! The immigration of people from an entirely different world, people with hatred in their hearts, has shattered that once great country,” Donald Trump said in a post on his Truth Social platform. “Close your Borders and take control, before it is too late!”
Iran and Hungary followed suit.
Shell-shocked, Emmanuel Macron , the French president, broke his silence to issue a frankly laughable promise that all masked and black-clad looters would be “pursued and punished”.
Sebastien Lecornu, the French president’s embattled prime minister, called on the French to choose sides between “the Republic or the rioters”.
But it was another political choice that was on most French people’s minds.
Mr Macron has only six months left in the Elysée Palace before his second and final presidential term ends.
One wonders whether such a fractured country has the patience to wait that long to choose his replacement.
While France, and the wider world, waits to see if the country jolts to the Right or Left, it is unlikely that whoever takes the reins in April will be as equivocal as the incumbent leader.
The French president addressed the nation on Sunday night, saying that public gatherings would be banned to halt rioting if necessary.
He pledged that there would be harsh consequences for the “criminals” who were looting and burning, and said they must “never” be confused with the peaceful protesters. “They will answer for what they have done to the Republic,” he added.
But the current revolt has stripped the 48-year-old centrist of his last fig leaf of domestic political capital since his disastrous decision to call snap elections in 2024.
In the ensuing period, France has lurched like a headless cockerel from one domestic crisis to another, run by a minority government barely able to pass a budget.
With the costs of the riots running into the “hundreds of millions” and the state more cash-strapped than ever, the age-old Gallic reflex of whipping out the cheque book to quell unrest – such as during the 2018 Yellow Vest revolt – is no longer an option.
In its defence, the French government plaintively asserts that education spending has risen during the Macron presidency, including by around 5 per cent in real terms since 2019. It is proposing a further €1.2bn (£1bn) increase next year.
However, it also plans to abolish almost 1,600 permanent teaching posts, while pension costs consume nearly a third of the education ministry’s budget. Universities have fared worse, with funding per student falling sharply since Mr Macron took office.
But even if the government could stump up more cash, the demands are now so diffuse that forking out more is unlikely to make much difference.
Deprived of the normal levers, Mr Lecornu pointed the finger squarely at the “extreme Left”, saying it was no coincidence that groups had targeted “centres of power” on Saturday. Many protesters took up social media calls to storm the parliament and the Elysée Palace – to no avail.
“Clearly this is a political manoeuvre,” Mr Lecornu claimed.
The unnamed culprit is Jean-Luc Mélenchon , firebrand leader of the Leftist France Unbowed.
Polls suggest the 75-year-old putative revolutionary could reach the presidential run-off against the National Rally’s Marine Le Pen next May – even if the latest place him on a par with Raphael Glucksmann, the Socialist, and Edouard Philippe, the centre-Right former prime minister.
Mr Mélenchon has shamelessly blown hot and cold, accusing the government and police of being the cause of all the damage before issuing a late-night call for calm, almost as an afterthought. In his defence, many pupils and students say he is the only one who has stuck up for them.
The Le Pen camp, meanwhile, hopes to capitalise on the unrest with a pledge to restore order.
Ms Le Pen said the troubles showed that Mr Macron’s administration was “running on fumes, exhausted and disoriented”.
“We are experiencing a profound crisis of trust and authority, which poses a threat to democracy,” said Ms Le Pen, who leads opinion polls ahead of the election.
Commentators point to the May 1968 mass protests that Charles de Gaulle decried as “la chienlit” (bed defecation, in other words, bedlam). In their wake, the French Right won a huge parliamentary majority.
“Macron’s 10 years end in absolute chaos. The Left is guilty, Macronistes are accomplices. Vote!” headlined RN spin doctors in a social media edit of the worst of the violence.
Mr Macron may be a busted flush. But to claim Mr Mélenchon – who is gunning for young voters and the high-immigrant banlieues – is somehow controlling this mayhem is fanciful. He is merely fanning the flames of a far wider anger smouldering in this combustible and divided nation.
As one editorialist put it: “The chaos in the streets reflects the chaos in [French] heads.”
The question is whether any presidential candidate is in a position to address it.

articles.title_orig: Rubio heads to Central Asia as some wonder if he's keeping the most pressing matters at a distance
articles.title_zh: Rubio heads to Central Asia as some wonder if he's keeping the most pressing matters at a distance
articles.content_orig:
United States Secretary of State Marco Rubio is to visit India in the coming week, but he will not set foot in the capital, New Delhi.
Instead, on Monday, Rubio will hold talks with Indian External Affairs Minister Subrahmanyam Jaishankar in Mumbai, India’s financial hub, and then visit an oil refinery in Jamnagar in the western state of Gujarat, according to a statement from the US Department of State.
His itinerary sparked a political storm after the US ambassador to India said Washington expected Jaishankar to travel to meet Rubio, prompting opposition leaders to accuse the government of allowing India’s top diplomat to be “summoned” on home soil.
The spat comes as relations between the two countries are strained over trade, tariffs and India’s purchases of Russian oil.
So why is Rubio avoiding New Delhi, and why has it caused such upset? Here’s what you need to know:
He plans to discuss trade, energy and investment.
Rubio is arriving on Sunday from Samarkand, Uzbekistan, where he has been meeting with five Central Asian states at the C5+1 summit .
In India, he is due to meet senior officials to discuss the US-India strategic partnership and energy cooperation and hold talks with business leaders, the State Department said.
Indian Ministry of External Affairs spokesperson Randhir Jaiswal appeared to confirm the agenda, stating on Friday that the Mumbai talks would cover energy, trade and investment, defence, and critical and emerging technologies.
In Jamnagar, Rubio is to visit the world’s largest single-site refinery, operated by billionaire Mukesh Ambani’s Reliance Industries, and attend a reception hosted by the Ambani family, according to The Hindu newspaper.
No official reason has been given.
Rubio was in the Indian capital in May for a meeting of foreign ministers of countries in the Quad, a group consisting of the US, India, Japan and Australia.
The State Department has framed his upcoming trip around energy and investment, and the second stop on Rubio’s India visit, Jamnagar, is one of the world’s most important energy hubs.
The visit also comes as fuel prices bite in the US before next month’s midterm elections.
Reliance, an energy, retail and telecommunications conglomerate, also sits at the centre of Washington’s wider oil diplomacy .
Business Standard, an Indian financial daily, said the Jamnagar stop was significant because Reliance is the biggest buyer of Venezuelan crude oil besides the US at a time when Washington has been urging India to buy more.
Since US forces seized Venezuelan President Nicolas Maduro in January and took essential control of the country’s oil industry, the US government has marketed Venezuelan oil to buyers abroad.
Reliance is also investing in a new refinery in Texas, the first to be built in the US in 50 years, which Trump hailed as a $300bn deal when he announced it in March, Business Standard reported.
Speaking at the Bloomberg New Economy Forum in New Delhi on Thursday, US Ambassador to India Sergio Gor said Rubio would meet Indian government officials in Mumbai, and Washington “expected” Jaishankar and others from New Delhi to travel there to see him.
Earlier in the week, however, Jaiswal had not confirmed the trip or explained why Rubio was skipping New Delhi, telling reporters the Indian government would announce it “at the appropriate time”, The Hindu newspaper reported.
Jairam Ramesh, a general secretary of the opposition Indian National Congress party, wrote on X that the ambassador’s statement was “quite extraordinary”.
Rahul Gandhi, leader of the opposition in parliament’s lower house, also took to X to comment, writing on Friday that Rubio had “summoned his employee to Mumbai”.
Congress MP Pawan Khera went further.
“A foreign government summoning India’s External Affairs Minister on Indian soil is a new low, even by the Modi Government’s standards,” he wrote on X, referring to Prime Minister Narendra Modi.
Mainly because of Trump’s tariffs and Russian oil.
In August last year after a round of trade talks broke down, the US hit most Indian goods with a 50 percent tariff. Under a framework the two sides agreed in February, that rate fell to 18 percent, however.
Since then, negotiations have stalled.
This month, Indian Finance Minister Nirmala Sitharaman said the talks had “plateaued”, according to The Hindu.
On Thursday, Trade Minister Piyush Goyal said the “first tranche” of a deal was in its final stages but India would not sign until its exporters had an edge over rivals such as Bangladesh, Vietnam and Indonesia, according to the Reuters news agency.
Other points of friction have emerged.
Last week, US Labor Secretary Keith Sonderling announced that his department was suspending eight companies – including the Indian IT giants Infosys, Tata Consultancy Services, Wipro and HCL – from a labour certification scheme that is a key step for employers seeking green cards for their foreign staff.
Sameer Lalwani, a senior fellow in the South Asia Program at the Carnegie Endowment for International Peace, wrote this week that Indian public opinion of the US has hit a record low, citing US engagement with Pakistan and the US-Israel war on Iran, which he said had pushed India back towards Russian oil.
Despite that, he argued, defence and technology cooperation has quietly deepened, and bilateral trade grew by almost 12 percent in 2025 to nearly $240bn.
In his view, “perceptions of the political relationship have deteriorated faster than its strategic foundations.”
A sanctions law had threatened to make matters worse.
Last month, Trump signed the Lindsey O Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act, which could impose tariffs of up to 100 percent on goods from the five largest importers of Russian oil or gas.
India, one of the world’s biggest buyers of Russian oil, had warned Washington that new tariffs could hurt bilateral ties. Trump signed an executive order seeking to waive the sanctions on Friday as he tries to ease high oil prices before the November 3 US elections.

articles.title_orig: Canadian military base fire: Death toll confirmed and cause under investigation
articles.title_zh: Canadian military base fire: Death toll confirmed and cause under investigation
articles.content_orig:
The busy training base is located behind fences on remote land in Alberta
A huge fire swept through a Canadian military base on Saturday, killing at least four people and leaving 19 people in critical condition.
Prime Minister Mark Carney described it as one of the worst peace time tragedies on Canadian soil in the history of the military.
Here is what we know about the deadly incident so far.
The fire at Canadian Forces Base Wainwright broke out at around 16:00 local time (22:00 GMT).
Major-General Wade Rutland, Commander of 1st Canadian Division, said a grass fire ignited on a training range and "uncommonly strong winds caused it to spread rapidly and shift direction" towards soldiers taking part in exercises.
He said the cause of the initial fire remains under investigation.
Earlier, local media reported it may have been started when a gas main was struck during a live firing exercise, but the military later said that investigators do not believe any explosions were caused by oil or gas infrastructure.
Carney described the fire as "violent" and "fast-moving".
The prime minister said military and civilian fire crews "fought this fire throughout the night in some of the worst conditions imaginable, risking their lives to protect their fellow Canadians".
The Canadian defence ministry has said the cause remains under investigation, and "at this time, there are no indications that it was the result of any terrorist activity".
Carney: 'Canada must now serve' service members killed in fire
Four service members are confirmed to have died, while a further 39 people are in hospital - 19 of whom are in critical condition.
Officials have not indicated whether or not the government expects the death toll to rise but said many people had suffered severe burns.
On Saturday evening, Royal Alexandra Hospital in Edmonton declared a code orange - a disaster response protocol for a high-casualty incident. It was stood down on Sunday afternoon.
Alberta's health service said the emergency response lasted for 10 hours, and involved 22 ambulances and eight aircraft.
Ongoing care for the injured is expected to be "intensive", a statement continued.
A stream of ambulances were seen arriving at the hospital and one doctor told Canadian public broadcaster CBC that the facility had been "completely overwhelmed" by the number of patients.
Canadian Forces Base Wainwright is located in a rural area of the western province of Alberta - around 120 miles (193km) from Edmonton and 180 miles (290km) from Calgary, the province's two largest cities.
It is one of Canadian Army's busiest military training bases and its airfield is also used by the Royal Canadian Air Force.
It population fluctuates but more than 1,000 people can be based there at any given time.

articles.title_orig: Macron calls for calm in France and warns rioting must not escalate
articles.title_zh: Macron calls for calm in France and warns rioting must not escalate
articles.content_orig:
Watch: James Waterhouse speaks to looted shop owners on the streets of Paris
French President Emmanuel Macron has called for "calm and order" after a major day of protests turned into rioting and looting on Saturday, and as some disorder continued in Paris on Sunday.
In a national address from the ÃlysÃ©e Palace, he warned those who had taken part not to "escalate", adding: "We all feel anger and shame."
Some 550,000 demonstrators took to the streets for largely peaceful protests against rising fuel prices, the cost of living and deteriorating public services, including schools.
Macron said a distinction must be drawn between the "legitimate demands" of protesters and "those who destroyed, smashed and looted".
Police have arrested about 2,400 people, according to France's interior ministry.
The French president said "nothing justifies" the "unbridled" violence seen and said those involved would face justice.
Groups of rioters, some dressed in black and wearing masks and balaclavas, also came out in Paris, Marseille and other towns and cities, with some setting fire to cars and buildings.
Local officials said the Limoges town hall was "largely lost" after fire caused part of the building to collapse
On Sunday, looting and clashes with police continued on a smaller scale in parts of the capital and Lyon.
Tear gas and stun grenades were fired at hundreds of people in Paris, according to the AFP news agency, and bottles and rocks were again hurled at police.
Sunday saw cities across the country confront the impact of what developed into one of the worst bouts of disorder in modern French history.
In Limoges, the ornate 19th Century city hall was gutted by a fire started by rioters on Saturday, its clock tower and roof collapsing and the flames took hold.
A view of the damage inside Limoges town hall on Sunday morning
Speaking near the ruined building, AnnÃ¨yse said: "This is very upsetting. Harming heritage buildings just because you are angry at the government is selfish, I think. It's hurting everybody."
"It's awful and unbelievable," said another man who gave his name as Gerrard. "We are very sad and I think it will be a long time to put it back as it was before."
Shopkeepers were seen early on Sunday morning picking up large shards of glass in Paris as rubbish trucks cleared up debris on some of the larger streets.
Fires were lit and shops looted during smaller scale disorder in Paris on Sunday
Widespread looting took place across the cities of Paris, Marseille and Lille, as well as other areas.
Macron said local prefects and mayors would draft measures to protect shops and civic buildings.
The president also said there would be "full transparency" over the police response to the demonstrations.
Tear gas and water cannon were turned on crowds over the weekend and riot police were seen hitting people with batons in several places.
France's interior ministry said about 1,000 police officers were injured on Saturday, seven of them seriously.
A man tries to extinguish a fire in Paris on Sunday
Student protests which began last month escalated significant on Saturday after they were joined by trade union members and other anti-government groups.
The response from political figures has pointed to France's deep political divisions as the country prepares for an election in April which could see the hard-right pitted against the hard-left.
France's Interior Minister Laurent NuÃ±ez said that while demonstrating was a fundamental right, there were "outrages" committed by "several thousand far-left individuals" who were determined to target public buildings and confront the police.
Later, they were joined by "delinquents who looted and ransacked numerous businesses in several cities in France", he said.
Jean-Luc MÃ©lenchon - leader of the hard-left La France Insoumise party - heavily criticised NuÃ±ez and police chiefs on social media.
He said they had "shown complete incompetence" with their handling of the demonstrations and called them "specialists in organised chaos".
Meanwhile, the leader of the hard-right National Rally party, Marine Le Pen, condemned the "exploitation" of anger "by political forces that encourage violence".

articles.title_orig: Austrian Airlines flight from Tel Aviv to Vienna lands in Sofia after reported bomb threat
articles.title_zh: Austrian Airlines flight from Tel Aviv to Vienna lands in Sofia after reported bomb threat
articles.content_orig:
An Airbus A320 flight from Tel Aviv to Vienna has made an emergency landing in Bulgaria following a reported bomb threat, according to the Bulgarian Ministry of Transport.
Austrian Airlines flight OS82 was near the border with Romania when the crew received a bomb threat and decided to land in the Bulgarian capital, Sofia, the Transport Ministry said in a statement on Sunday.
Bulgaria’s Ministry of Defence said an air force MiG-29 fighter jet escorted the plane to Sofia airport.
Initial information showed the aircraft carried six crew members and 51 passengers, all of whom have all since disembarked, according to the Transport Ministry’s statement.
The airline told the AFP news agency that a security search of the aircraft was conducted.
“Once the search of the aircraft is complete, the passengers will be rebooked onto alternative flights as quickly as possible,” the airline said.
A crisis response team has been set up, and relevant authorities have launched an investigation into the incident, the Bulgarian Transport Ministry said.
According to aviation and flight tracking site FlightAware, Austrian Airlines 82 left the Ben Gurion airport in Tel Aviv on Sunday at 6:46pm local time (15:46 GMT) and landed about three hours later at Vasil Levski airport in Sofia at 9:43pm (18:43 GMT).
Flightradar24 data showed it entered Romanian airspace at about 9:10pm (18:10 GMT) before turning south and heading back towards Bulgaria.
Information from the flight-tracking platform ADS-B Exchange indicates the aircraft was transmitting squawk code 7700 – a signal for a general emergency – at around the same time.
Last month, a Flydubai plane carrying 174 passengers was on its way from the United Arab Emirates to Tel Aviv when a co-pilot allegedly attacked the pilot with an axe in an attempt to crash the plane.
The aircraft plunged about 17,000 feet (5,180 metres) before it was brought back under control by other Flydubai pilots after passengers and other crew subdued the alleged attacker.
The flight was diverted and forced to make an emergency landing at Prince Sultan bin Abdulaziz International Airport in Tabuk, northwestern Saudi Arabia.
Authorities in the UAE said the co-pilot was on a “suicide” mission to crash the plane at Israel’s Ben Gurion airport in Tel Aviv.
The co-pilot, Hamam Al-Hammami , an Omani national, has since been charged with terrorism offences in the UAE.
The Israeli government responded to the incident by ordering checks on the identities of all pilots flying into the country.

articles.title_orig: Exclusive: NVIDIA’s Vera Team Says Chiplet Designs Sacrificed Single-Threaded Performance For Core Counts, And Agentic AI Is Now Forcing A Reversal
articles.title_zh: Exclusive: NVIDIA’s Vera Team Says Chiplet Designs Sacrificed Single-Threaded Performance For Core Counts, And Agentic AI Is Now Forcing A Reversal
articles.content_orig:
After years of AI infrastructure talk revolving around GPUs, Google Cloud’s Mark Lohmeyer told Fierce CPUs are poised for something of a comeback.
The reason? Agentic AI workloads don’t behave like the chatbots that kicked off the generative AI boom. Instead of taking a prompt and returning an answer in one shot, agents are expected to spin up other agents, call APIs, access enterprise applications and data, write and run code, and preserve context across sessions that could stretch for days, weeks or even months.
“All of that requires CPUs,” Lohmeyer, who is the company’s VP and GM for AI and Computing Infrastructure, said. While inference will still lean on GPUs and TPUs, Lohmeyer said the orchestration layer around agentic workloads will drive “a ton of additional demand for CPUs.”
Lohmeyer isn’t the only one who thinks so. AMD has been banging the CPU drum for more than a year now and Red Hat also told Fierce CPUs will likely play a key role in inferencing and AI orchestration.
This shift is driving two big changes. First, the Lohmeyer said Google Cloud is designing a new class of compute services capable of handling workloads that are highly bursty, frequently idle and that need to preserve their state over long periods. These would allow customers to spin up compute when agents need it, hibernate that compute when they don’t, and restart it quickly without losing context. It’s a win-win: customers avoid paying for time when their compute is idle, while still maintaining the ability to keep long-running agentic sessions intact.
But if you’re wondering how on earth Google Cloud – or any other provider, for that matter – can juggle many such workloads on finite compute resources, so were we. Lohmeyer said the shift toward agentic AI is also driving a rethink of how workloads are packed onto physical infrastructure (i.e. hardware). It’s all about upping utilization and maximizing resource use. Indeed, Red Hat’s Steve Watt told Fierce in May that CPU rates are notoriously low and noted the Intel and AMD-led x86 Ecosystem Advisory Group is trying to solve for this very problem.
Here’s how it could work, in theory: If an agent only needs to actively run 5% or 10% of the time, cloud providers may be able to support a high density of agentic workloads on the same physical infrastructure while keeping environments secure and separate using sandboxes.
“Basically all of those agents will run in some type of sandbox. So, it could be a VM, it could be a microVM, it could be a container that basically isolates that specific workload,” Lohmeyer explained. “We think this actually becomes really, really important for the industry because as the demand continues to rise, you want to make the most effective use of those underlying compute and memory and other resources. That ability to consolidate, let's say 10 to one or higher we think is going to be really important to meet the scale that our customers expect.”
Though Lohmeyer didn’t mention the Advisory Group’s work on CPU utilization, he noted during the conversation that Google Cloud has deep partnerships with both AMD and Intel to run x86-based instances, alongside Google’s own Arm-based Axion CPU instances.
Lohmeyer isn’t ready to say agentic AI demands an entirely new class of CPU. However, he did note the workload is different enough that cloud providers will need to rethink how CPUs, storage, networking and orchestration software are designed together.
He described co-design as one of the more important principles for the agentic era — not just tuning the CPU itself, but optimizing the hardware and software stack around workloads that can hibernate for long stretches, preserve state outside active memory and then restart en masse when demand returns.
“How it flows down into specific chip architecture is probably a little bit early for that, but I think this idea of codesign is going to be important just like it has been for GPUs and TPUs and the software stuck on top of them,” he said. “The same thing I think will be true here.”
As enterprises hustle to get compute ready for the agentic future, Lohmeyer said they need to be thinking about more than just what it takes to run the agents. They need to make sure their other infrastructure – APIs, data sources, interconnectivity – is up to snuff.
“Yes, you need the optimal infrastructure for the agent itself. But then that has repercussions for the rest of the applications and data and the infrastructure that powers those in the enterprise, because it's going to be accessing it with different types of patterns than we've seen in the past,” Lohmeyer said.
That, Lohmeyer concluded, will force enterprises to rethink not only how they scale those back-end platforms, but where they locate data and applications so they sit closer to where the agents are running.

articles.title_orig: Bond Market’s Big Short Bet Gets Wakeup Call as AI Trade Wobbles
articles.title_zh: Bond Market’s Big Short Bet Gets Wakeup Call as AI Trade Wobbles
articles.content_orig:
U.S. Treasury yields teetered on Friday as investors weighed hotter-than-expected inflation data and Federal Reserve Chairman Kevin Warsh's latest comments on interest rates.
The benchmark 10-year Treasury yield fell less than 1 basis point to 5.085%, while the 30-year Treasury bond yield rose less than 1 basis point to 5.434%. The 2-year Treasury note yield was down more than 3 basis points at 4.715%.
One basis point is equal to 0.01%, and yields and prices move in opposite directions.
It's been a week of strong inflation data, with Thursday's producer price index showing that wholesale prices jumped 6.3% annually in September, the biggest gain since 2022, according to the Bureau of Labor Statistics. Economists polled by Dow Jones expected a 5.5% increase.
This came after the Wednesday release of the consumer price index, which rose 0.6% for the month and 3.7% annually in September, against estimates of 0.6% and 3.6%, respectively.
The rise has largely been driven by continued inflationary pressure from soaring energy prices amid the ongoing U.S.-Iran war.
The inflation data comes two weeks ahead of the next interest rate decision, with Fed Chairman Warsh on Thursday declining to offer any signals as to whether there will be another interest rate hike this month.
"I don't prejudge meetings. I don't believe in saying now what I might do at the meetings that we have in the balance of this year," Warsh said.
Traders are now pricing in a more than 80% chance that the Fed will hold rates, according to the CME FedWatch Tool .

articles.title_orig: Super Typhoon Champi intensifies to a Cat 5 after battering Guam
articles.title_zh: Super Typhoon Champi intensifies to a Cat 5 after battering Guam
articles.content_orig:
After lashing Guam as a Cat 4 super typhoon with 150 mph (240 km/h) winds, Super Typhoon Champi intensified just six hours later – at 0Z Sunday, October 18 – into a formidable Cat 5 with sustained winds of 165 mph (265 km/h), said the Joint Typhoon Warning Center (JTWC). The center of Super Typhoon Champi passed about 12 miles (20 km) south of Guam’s southern tip around 18Z (2 p.m. EDT) Saturday, Oct. 17. The northern eyewall barely grazed Guam’s southern tip, so the island escaped catastrophic wind damage.
JTWC initially analyzed Champi as a Cat 4 with 150 mph winds at 00 UTC Oct. 18, but in a subsequent forecast discussion, they noted they had reanalyzed the 0Z intensity, upgrading it to Cat 5. Champi is the ninth Cat 5 observed globally so far in 2026 (see below).
An eyewall replacement cycle significantly weakened Champi after its surge to Cat 5 strength. By 15Z (11 a.m. EDT) Sunday, Champi’s peak sustained winds were estimated to be 140 mph (225 km/h). The storm is projected to track steadily west-northwest this week, approaching the vicinity of Taiwan by week’s end. With exceptionally favorable conditions along its path for the next several days – light to moderate wind shear, a moist atmosphere, ample upper-level outflow, and unusually warm sea surface temperatures of 29-30 degrees Celsius (84-86 degrees Fahrenheit) – Champi is predicted by JTWC to regain Cat 5 status on Monday and to remain near the Cat 4/5 threshold into midweek.
6.5 hours of #Champi 's violent pinhole eyewall on visible imagery. Notice not only the continued core contraction, but also the particularly pronounced standing gravity wave in the southern CDO at close to peak intensity — fascinating stuff pic.twitter.com/ONFZjRJoGF
Guam (pop. 170,000) has extensive experience with typhoons. According to the NOAA historical hurricane tracks website , from 1948-2025, no fewer than 27 typhoons of category 1 or higher passed within 50 miles of Guam; 14 were major Cat 3 or stronger storms. Champi is the second major typhoon this year to come within 50 miles (80 km) of Guam, after Super Typhoon Bavi , which passed about 45 miles (75 km) north of Guam on July 5 at peak strength with 180 mph (285 km/h) winds. In addition, Cat 4 Typhoon Sinlaku passed about 110 miles (175 km) north of Guam on April 14.
According to EM-DAT, the international disasters database, the strongest and most destructive typhoon to hit Guam was Typhoon Karen of 1962, which hit the island Nov. 11 as a category 5 storm with 170 mph (275 km/h) winds, killing six and doing $2.9 billion in damage (2026 dollars). Guam’s deadliest typhoon was Pamela of 1976, which hit May 21 as a category 4 storm with 140 mph (225 km/h) winds, killing nine and doing over $700 million in damage.
Super Typhoon Bavi passed about 2 miles (3 km) north of Rota Island in the U.S. Northern Mariana Islands on July 5 when at peak strength with 180 mph (285 km/h) winds. The storm’s large eye completely encompassed the island. Although no fatalities were reported, the mayor of Rota described the island as having been damaged or destroyed “in every aspect” by Bavi. Passing well north of the Philippines as a Category 1 storm several days later, Bavi triggered heavy rains and landslides that killed 23 people and left 18 missing across the Philippines. Bavi later hit China as a Category 1 storm with 90 mph (150 km/h) winds on July 12. Technically, we can’t credit Bavi with making landfall in Rota (and thus the U.S.), since the center of the eye passed 2 miles north of the island. But regardless of technicalities, Bavi was catastrophic for Rota. Damage from the storm has not yet been quantified.
Super Typhoon Sinlaku peaked with 185 mph (295 km/hr) winds a few hundred miles southeast of Guam on April 12, making the typhoon Earth’s strongest storm of 2026. Sinlaku weakened to a Cat 4 with sustained winds of 145 mph (230 km/hr) at landfall in the U.S. Northern Mariana Islands on April 14, with the storm’s large eye passing over both Tinian and Saipan simultaneously. Sinlaku killed 17. Sinlaku is being blamed for $458 million in damage to Guam, and over $1 billion in damage to the U.S. Northern Mariana Islands.
Sinlaku was the 10th Category 4 or 5 tropical cyclone to make landfall in a U.S. state or territory in the past 10 years; that’s as many Cat 4 and Cat 5 landfalls as the U.S. Gulf and Atlantic coast suffered over the prior 57 years.
Counting Champi, at least eight Category 5 tropical cyclones have developed around the world in 2026, and perhaps nine if Choi-Wan is confirmed (see below). The others to date:
The 1990-2025 average yearly number of Category 5 storms globally was 5.3; there were five in 2025 (Hurricanes Melissa, Erin, and Humberto in the Atlantic; Typhoon Ragasa in the Northwest Pacific; and Cyclone Errol in the South Indian Ocean).
As seen in Fig. 3, 2026 is now tied for third place for the most Cat 5s globally in a year since accurate satellite records began in 1982 (assuming Choi-Wan ends up being a Cat 5). (Note that some of 2026’s low-end Cat 5s may be downgraded to Cat 4 in post-season analysis, and two near-Cat 5s with 155 mph winds in the eastern Pacific, Hurricane Nolo and Hurricane Simon, may be upgraded to Cat 5.) The number of Cat 5s has increased globally since accurate global satellite data became available in 1982 (this increase is statistically significant at the 99.5% level). Numerous studies over the past 20 years have found that hurricane-strength storms are not becoming more numerous globally, but the fraction of such storms that reach Category 4 or 5 strength is growing and expected to keep growing, so the world is seeing more of these intense tropical cyclones, which tend to be the most deadly and destructive ones.
Hurricane Trudy borrowed the script from its immediate predecessor, Hurricane Simon, as it passed near the coast of Mexico’s Jalisco state on Saturday night while its center remained just offshore. As of 11 a.m. EDT Sunday, Cat 2 Trudy was centered about 115 mi (185 km) southwest of Cabo Corrientes, heading northwest at 8 mph (13 km/h) with top sustained winds of 105 mph. Hurricane warnings had been lifted, though tropical storm warnings remained in effect. Trudy’s gale-force sustained winds extended just onshore at times over the weekend, but hurricane-force winds have remained well offshore. The Jalisco coast could experience 4-6 inches (100-150 mm) of additional rain from Trudy on Sunday as the storm angles offshore and weakens , likely dissipating by midweek.
Yet another tropical cyclone is likely to develop later this week in the Eastern Pacific from a disturbance off the coast of Central America. Model ensembles suggest that any such system could recurve toward the northwest Mexican coast by next weekend or beyond. In its Tropical Weather Outlook issued at midday Sunday, the NOAA/NWC National Hurricane Center gave this system a 90% chance of development in the 2- to 7-day window.
A slow-moving storm off the East Coast of the U.S. could bring several days of strong winds, coastal flooding and beach erosion, forecasters said, with parts of the Mid-Atlantic facing the greatest risk through later in the week.
NHC is also keeping its eye on a nor’easter-type low developing off the Carolinas on Sunday and Monday. The surface low is linked to an upper-level disturbance that was getting pinched off and left behind by a stronger, higher-latitude trough passing by well to the north. This cut-off system will meander for several days as it gradually organizes over unusually warm water for mid-October, pushing strong winds against the coast and prolonging high water. Several days of at least minor to moderate coastal flooding with breaking waves of 8-13 feet can be expected, especially from the Outer Banks of North Carolina to the Delmarva peninsula and southern New Jersey.
